title: Providing Minimal-Sized Responses to DNS Queries That Have QTYPE=ANY
summary: Gives guidance on how authoritative DNS servers can respond to QTYPE=ANY queries with minimal-sized answers, since operators may choose not to give full responses for security or performance reasons. The DNS specification had no specific advice for this.

eli5.summary: If someone asks for everything you know, you may reply with just one small thing. This explains good ways to give a short answer.

questions: how to respond to qtype any
what is a dns any query
why do dns servers return hinfo for any queries
how do dns amplification attacks use any
subtitle: How a DNS server can answer an ANY query with one small record instead of everything it knows.

tldr.problem: A DNS query with QTYPE=ANY asks for all records at a name, which can produce large responses. Those are useful to attackers for amplification and costly for servers, and the DNS specification gave no guidance on declining them.
tldr.mechanism: A responder may answer with a single RRset or a small subset, a synthesized HINFO record whose CPU field is "RFC8482", or a best guess at the likely wanted records. Initiators can cache the result and stop asking.
tldr.outcome: The behavior is optional, and it updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035. It makes servers less attractive as amplifiers in reflection attacks.

today: RFC 8482 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it in the metadata. Following it is optional.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) has a query type (QTYPE) called ANY, which is type code 255, written "*" in RFC 1035. The operator of an authoritative server might choose not to answer such queries in full, for reasons of local policy, security or performance.

The DNS specification (RFC 1034 and RFC 1035) gave no guidance for that situation. This document supplies it. It calls the host sending a request the initiator and the host sending the response the responder. A conventional ANY response is one built by the algorithm in Section 4.3.2 of RFC 1034 with none of this document's mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a computer asks a name server for everything it knows about a name. The rules did not say what to do if the server would rather not hand over a giant list. This document says.

sections.title: Why ANY Queries Are Used
sections.content:
ANY queries have legitimate uses. They help with debugging and with checking the state of a server for a name. Some people use them to save queries, for example to get the MX, A and AAAA RRsets for a mail domain in one go. There is no documented guidance for that use, and the RFC says some implementations have been observed not to work as their developers expected. Anyone who relies on ANY should include a fallback.

They also have abusive uses:

  • ANY queries are frequently used to exploit the amplification potential of DNS servers using spoofed source addresses and UDP. Small responses make a server a less attractive amplifier.
  • They can be used to mine authoritative-only servers for zone data, since they are expected to return all RRsets for a name.
  • Some authoritative-only servers need extra processing to build a conventional ANY response, which operators may want to avoid.
sections.eli5: Asking for everything is handy for checking things. But bad people can use it to make a server send a huge pile of data at someone else, so servers want a way to keep the answer small.

sections.title: The General Approach
sections.content:
The proposal lets an authoritative server signal that conventional ANY queries are not supported for a particular QNAME. It does this in a way that works with unmodified clients such as resolvers, and triggers the behavior wanted from them.

The RFC says that other approaches were discussed. One proposed a new RCODE to signal that the server did not answer ANY in the standard way. That had an undesirable effect: a resolver receiving an unknown RCODE would resend the same query to all available authoritative servers instead of suppressing future ANY queries for that name. Returning a non-empty RRset avoids this, because the resolver has something to cache, which suppresses repeat queries to the same or different servers.
sections.eli5: Instead of saying "I will not answer", the server gives a small real answer. The asker writes it down and does not keep pestering anyone.

sections.title: How Responders Answer
sections.content:
For queries where the QNAME exists, QCLASS=IN and QTYPE=ANY, the RFC describes three modes, and operators and implementers may choose whichever suits them. Except as described, the responder MUST follow the standard algorithms.

Subset of RRsets (4.1). The responder MAY decline to give a conventional response and MAY send a single RRset, or a larger subset, in the answer section. Where several RRsets exist, it SHOULD choose a small subset to reduce amplification. If the zone is signed, the appropriate RRSIG records MUST be included. There is no signal telling the client the answer is incomplete.

Synthesized HINFO (4.2). If no CNAME exists at the name, the responder MAY synthesize one HINFO record. Its CPU field SHOULD be "RFC8482" and its OS field SHOULD be the null string, to keep the response small. The TTL SHOULD be large enough to suppress frequent repeat ANY queries from the same initiator for the same QNAME, but not so long that changing the policy later is hard, and it SHOULD be configurable. If DO=1 and the zone is known to be signed, a valid RRSIG MUST be returned; with DO=0 it SHOULD be omitted. Receivers SHOULD NOT assume an HINFO answer was synthesized under this specification.

Best guess (4.3). A responder can try to return what the initiator probably wants. Some implementations return all CNAME, MX, A and AAAA RRsets at the name and suppress others such as TXT and DNSKEY, which can make responses large. The result is generally larger than with the first two approaches. If the zone is signed and the DO bit is set, an RRSIG RRset MUST be included.

Transport (4.4). A responder MAY behave differently per transport, for example a conventional response over TCP while using one of the small-response methods over UDP.
sections.eli5: The server has three choices: give one small answer, give a made-up short note that says it is not answering, or guess the few things you most likely want. It may even give the full answer on a safer road, TCP, and the short one on UDP.

sections.title: Initiators and the HINFO Side Effect
sections.content:
An initiator that gets back an HINFO record or a single RRset MAY cache it in the normal way, following normal caching semantics. It MAY also suppress further ANY queries if its cache holds a matching HINFO record with the CPU field described in Section 4, or answer such queries from its cache.

There is a side effect. A cached synthesized HINFO RRset might suppress later queries for QTYPE=HINFO from the same initiator, effectively masking any real HINFO RRset in the zone. Operators whose zones use HINFO conventionally SHOULD choose the single-RRset method or another type. The RFC says HINFO is believed to be rarely used in the DNS at the time of writing, based on passive DNS and server observations.
sections.eli5: The asker keeps the short answer in a notebook and does not ask again for a while. The small catch is that the note could hide a real answer to a different question about the same name.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 1034 and RFC 1035
sections.content:
This document extends the processing of ANY queries in Section 4.3.2 of RFC 1034. It argues that returning a subset is legitimate and consistent with RFC 1035: it can be argued that ANY does not always mean ALL, as used in Section 3.2.3 of RFC 1035. The main difference is that the TC bit SHOULD NOT be set in the response, which signals that it is not a complete answer.

All of this is optional for both initiators and responders. RRSIG queries (QTYPE=RRSIG) can also cause large responses and extra work, but this RFC does not specify behavior for them, though future advice might benefit from consistency with these approaches.
sections.eli5: Nothing breaks the old rules. "Any" never really promised "all", and nobody has to follow the new advice.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Experience
sections.content:
ANY queries are frequently seen in reflection attacks, since a relatively small query can bring a large response. Being able to suppress those responses makes a server a less useful amplifier. The RFC states the optional behavior is compatible with DNSSEC for both initiator and responder.

On implementation experience, the RFC reports that the Cloudflare authoritative nameserver implemented the HINFO response in October 2015, with a few minor problems since resolved. NSD 4.1 implemented the subset mode in 2016. BIND9 got a single-RRset response, available in production releases starting in BIND 9.11.
sections.eli5: Bad guys like questions with tiny asks and giant answers. Making the answer small takes away the fun for them.
